posts.text:
By nature of being a vol trader, I’ve studied many different market crashes. Not just the common ones in the U.S., but episodes like Britain in 1720, Vienna in 1873, and the Dutch tulip mania of 1637.

There are some interesting behavioral takeaways that aren’t entirely intuitive unless you participate in markets every single day.

One of the biggest for me is that large market moves often need two-way action to develop. Behaviorally, you need participants willing to take the other side, because their eventual need to unwind can help accelerate the move. It’s almost like storing energy that gets released later. To create that dynamic, a “gray catalyst” can be particularly powerful one whose implications aren’t immediately black and white. 

Here are two examples that helped produce massive moves in opposite directions that had gray area headlines that led to that two way flow. 

COVID (March 2020): What often gets lost in the sauce is that many participants were aggressively betting against the idea that COVID would be severely disruptive. As stocks fell, they bought the dip and sold vol. When stocks kept falling and vol kept rising, some of those positions became fuel for the next leg of the move as participants were forced to unwind.

Looking back, the outcome seems obvious. In real time, the eventual scale of the disruption was far from clear. There was HOPE that it would pass quickly. Headlines about potential treatments, policy support, or a less severe impact repeatedly gave investors reasons to step back in. Stocks would rip 5% higher immediately on that news and hope, only to reverse again even lower when more negative news hit.

Those rallies matter. They give existing longs a reason to stay and new buyers a reason to enter. When the recovery fails, there is another round of positioning that may need to come out. Without that back-and-forth, it can be harder to produce the same degree of forced selling. The uncertainty helps keep replenishing the other side.

Meme mania (January 2021): Companies like GameStop and AMC surged hundreds of percent amid a speculative frenzy and short squeezes. Here, too, there was a gray area. Many investors saw businesses facing serious fundamental challenges, which made shorting them appear rational, especially as their share prices climbed further away from what those investors believed they were worth.

But a compelling fundamental argument does not tell you how far a stock can move before that argument pays off. As prices rose, some shorts covered, while others saw an even more attractive entry point and stepped in. That fresh short exposure created the potential for another round of forced buying if prices continued higher.

The gray area was the gap between the fundamental thesis and the path the market could take. Of course these weren’t great stocks, and the fact that people came in on that helped the waves move higher and higher. 

That’s the behavioral dynamic I find so interesting. Uncertainty can keep attracting participants to the other side of a move. As the move extends, their conviction runs into their capital constraints, and an opinion can turn into a forced transaction.

In early 2002, Elon was preparing to launch SpaceX and searching for the people who could help him build a rocket from scratch. One Sunday in January 2002, he walked into a friend's rented warehouse in Huntington Beach and found Tom Mueller holding an 80-pound rocket engine on his shoulder, trying to bolt it to a frame. It was the largest liquid-fuel engine any amateur had ever built, with 13,000 pounds of thrust, made in Tom's spare time. 

Elon asked the main question  “Could you build something bigger?”

The next Sunday Elon came to his house. It was Super Bowl Sunday; they watched maybe one play, because they were too busy sketching the first SpaceX rocket.

Tom became SpaceX employee #1, and the man who built engines on weekends went on to build Merlin, Kestrel and Draco. 

Elon saw a person, not a résumé, someone who built rockets with his own hands simply because he loved them.

"When we are listing a new project, for example, we want to look at the core business, like the business model, the investor and the team building it."

"Something a little bit sad is many good projects, like for example Circle, they don't issue a token, other than USDC, which is a token, but that's not like their platform token in the ICO term. They do an IPO."

"Many TradFi or RWA projects, or even some AI trading platforms, they may also just seek an IPO path rather than ICO path."

posts.text:
Crypto exchange volume dropped about 30% after the 10/10 crash

Bitget CEO Gracy Chen on where trading activity is moving, and why smaller exchanges were hit even harder

"Right after 10/10, we see a volume decrease of maybe 30% on average among all the top exchanges. For the smaller exchanges it could be even worse because there's like the Matthew effect."

"The big ones will become bigger, and the smaller ones will just shrink and become smaller and eventually die down. And that's indeed the situation that we've seen."

"What's quite interesting now that we are observing is a lot of users come to our platform to trade non-crypto assets. At its peak earlier this year, non-crypto assets counted for almost 40% of our total trading volume."

"One is tokenized commodities or commodity perpetuals, and the other one is stocks in general, especially US stocks."

posts.text:
Of the $388M stolen from Bitget, only $1-2M has been frozen so far

Bitget CEO Gracy Chen says crypto still struggles to trace stolen funds, while hackers shift from targeting keys to credentials

"They are more targeting credentials, processes, and trusted tools, rather than maybe originally mainly about private keys. Now we've done pretty good guarding of private keys, cold wallets, etc."

"But no exchange can address this alone. As an industry, we need to share intelligence around threats. We need to have a lot of fast coordination, especially when we are tracing illicit funds."

"On day one, you need to build your exchange with the mindset that they will be targeting you, especially if you grow bigger and have a lot of users and custodian funds."

posts.text: Great interview, looking forward to sharing the transcript of my own recent fireside chat with David Orr @orrdavid in early November.

quoted.text:
Hedge Fund Manager David Orr (@orrdavid) on why he’ll back a delivery guy over a Harvard grad, as long as the track record is real.

David Orr runs Militia Capital, a ~$480M hedge fund. ~50% annualized, Sharpe 2.

“If you didn’t go to Harvard, they’re not going to give you money. They’re gonna lead you on for years.”

We cover:
- Edge is just reps. He's placed a few hundred independent bets every year since 2019, more in one year than a lot of hedge fund managers get in a decade.
- The two-hour rule: if he can't decide on a stock in an hour or two, he skips it. When a trade goes against him, he quits. "The market said I'm wrong, I'm wrong."
- 500 positions in his partition and zero notes. Some of his best shorts are down 40% and he's forgotten what the company does.
- The Gogo lesson: he spent 100 hours on a short and was right on the fundamentals (it's now $2), but it ripped to $20 first. All that research made him stubborn on the way up.
- The AI risk system: it groups the book into custom baskets like "Banks Done Right" and "yield traps," recalculated daily. A 25% bet can quietly become 45% in two weeks.
- How Militia recruits PMs: 95% of track records are junk, and one cherry-picker ran 30 accounts and sent the best one. The PMs who make it include a game show winner, a Spanish government worker and a programmer, with 0.15 cross-correlation.
- The best short seller in the world, quietly: 40% a year short only for years, and he still gets a tiny allocation at his fund.
